lead: A control survey fixes a few points to a higher accuracy than the detail survey that follows. Horizontal control gives each point its easting and northing; vertical control gives its reduced level. Walls, roads, contours and drone maps are then hung on these points. An error in a detail point stays at that point, but an error in a control point is copied into everything fixed from it, so control is observed first, checked against a known value, adjusted, and only then used.
prereq: You need: triangulation and computing coordinates from Triangulation and trilateration, and benchmarks and closing errors from levelling.

sections.h3: Working from the whole to the part

blocks.text: The rule of surveying is to work from the whole to the part: first a sparse frame of strong control over the whole area, then denser and weaker control inside it, and detail last. Errors made in the small work then stay inside the frame instead of building up across the site. Two parties working from the same control also meet without a gap or an overlap.

Control is graded by order. National (first-order) control is fixed by the national survey with the best instruments and the strongest figures; second- and third-order points densify it; minor control on a site is fixed from those. Higher order means a smaller permitted error and wider spacing. Specifications differ, but as a guide a first-order traverse closes to about 1 in 25 000 or better and an ordinary theodolite traverse for an engineering site to about 1 in 5000 to 1 in 10 000.

Each control point is a permanent mark (a bolt in concrete, a pillar, a mark on a culvert) with a description: a sketch and measured distances to two or three nearby features, so it can be found and used again. Ground control points for drone and aerial mapping are control points that show clearly in the images and fix the photographs to the ground.

items: Triangulation: one measured base and observed angles; strong over hills and open country with long sights.
Trilateration: all sides measured by EDM; strong in scale, used with braced figures.
Traversing: a chain of measured lines and the angles between them; suits roads, canals, pipelines and built-up areas where a network of triangles cannot be seen through.
GNSS: satellite positioning at each station; stations need a clear sky but not a sight of each other, and give height as well.

blocks.text: A closed traverse either returns to its start (a loop) or ends on another known station, so its error can be found; an open traverse has no check and is not used for control. For a closed loop of n stations, the interior angles must sum to (2n − 4) × 90°. The angular error is shared equally among the angles; the whole-circle bearings are then computed from a known starting bearing (bearing of next line = bearing of previous line + 180° − interior angle, for a loop observed clockwise round the inside).

Departure = l sin β;   Latitude = l cos β
Closing error e = √[(ΣDep)² + (ΣLat)²];   relative precision = 1 in (Σl ÷ e)
Bowditch correction to a line = −(ΣDep or ΣLat) × l ÷ Σl
blocks.where: l is a line's length and β its whole-circle bearing. In a closed loop the departures and the latitudes must each sum to zero; what is left is the closing error. Bowditch's (compass) rule shares the error in proportion to the length of each line; it suits traverses where angles and distances are of similar precision. The transit rule shares it in proportion to each line's departure or latitude instead.

blocks.text: Vertical control is carried from benchmarks of the national levelling network by differential levelling in closed loops or between two benchmarks, with balanced sights. The closing error is the computed RL of the closing benchmark minus its known RL (for a loop, ΣBS − ΣFS, the sum of all backsights minus the sum of all foresights, which should be zero). It is accepted if it is within the permitted value C√K mm, K being the length of the run in km and C a constant set by the specification (a few millimetres for precise levelling, larger for ordinary work), and is then distributed in proportion to distance.

Where levelling is impractical (hill tops, across a gorge) trigonometric heights from reciprocal vertical angles give lower-order vertical control. GNSS gives heights above the ellipsoid, which must be turned into reduced levels with a geoid model before they can be used with benchmark heights.

examples.question: A closed theodolite traverse ABCD is run clockwise round the inside of a site to fix four control stations. The observed interior angles are B 95°35′20″, C 91°34′50″, D 84°13′20″ and A 88°37′10″. The bearing of AB is fixed at 48°20′00″ and A is at E 1000.000 m, N 2000.000 m. The lengths are AB 245.60, BC 198.35, CD 261.40 and DA 230.12 m. Adjust the angles, compute the bearings, the closing error and the relative precision, and find the adjusted coordinates of B, C and D by Bowditch's rule.
steps: Angle sum = 360°00′40″; for four stations it should be (2 × 4 − 4) × 90° = 360°. Error +40″, so subtract 10″ from each: B 95°35′10″, C 91°34′40″, D 84°13′10″, A 88°37′00″.
Departures (l sin β) and latitudes (l cos β), in m: AB +183.47, +163.27; BC +145.66, −134.63; CD −172.08, −196.77; DA −157.09, +168.16. Sums: ΣDep = −0.04 m, ΣLat = +0.03 m, over Σl = 935.47 m.
Closing error e = √(0.04² + 0.03²) = 0.05 m. Relative precision = 935.47 ÷ 0.05 = 1 in 18 700, better than 1 in 10 000, so the traverse is accepted.

Bowditch corrections (per metre: departure +0.04 ÷ 935.47, latitude −0.03 ÷ 935.47): departures +0.011, +0.008, +0.011, +0.010 m; latitudes −0.008, −0.006, −0.009, −0.007 m (each column rounded so that it sums to the error).
Adjusted departures and latitudes: AB +183.481, +163.262; BC +145.668, −134.636; CD −172.069, −196.779; DA −157.080, +168.153. Both columns now sum to zero.

traps: Starting detail before the control is closed and adjusted. An error found later cannot be removed from the detail already fixed.
Using (n − 2) × 180° for the wrong set of angles. It is the sum of interior angles; exterior angles of a loop sum to (2n + 4) × 90°.
Distributing the closing error with the same sign as the error. The correction has the opposite sign, so the sums become zero.
Quoting the closing error without the length. 0.05 m is excellent on 935 m and poor on 50 m; the relative precision 1 in (Σl ÷ e) is what is compared with the specification.
Adjusting a traverse whose closing error is beyond the limit. It is remeasured, not adjusted; adjustment shares only small random errors.

quiz.q: What is meant by working from the whole to the part?
quiz.a: Establishing a sparse frame of accurate control over the whole area first, then densifying it and finally fixing detail, so that errors in the small work are confined within the frame and do not build up.

quiz.q: Why is a traverse preferred to triangulation for the control of a city road?
quiz.a: Buildings and trees block the long sights a network of triangles needs, while a traverse needs a sight only to the next station along the road, and its lines follow the corridor to be mapped.

quiz.q: A traverse of total length 1250 m has ΣDep = +0.12 m and ΣLat = −0.09 m. Find the closing error and precision, and the Bowditch correction to the departure of a 300 m line.
A levelling loop of 9 km closes with ΣBS − ΣFS = −0.036 m. The permitted error is 12√K mm. Accept or reject, and give the correction per km.
quiz.a: Permitted = 12√9 = 36 mm; the error of 36 mm equals it, so the run just passes. Correction +36 ÷ 9 = +4 mm per km, applied in proportion to distance from the start.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the angular error was +40″ but the linear misclosure was only 0.05 m. Why are the angles adjusted before the coordinates are computed?
quiz.a: An unadjusted angular error turns every later bearing, so the misclosure would mix angle error with distance error and the Bowditch rule, which assumes small random errors in both, would distribute a systematic twist. Adjusting the angles first leaves only the linear error to share.

quiz.q: Should drone mapping of a 2 km² township rely on the drone's own GNSS, or on ground control points? Justify.
quiz.a: On ground control points, with some kept back as checks. On-board GNSS without correction fixes the camera to a few metres, so the whole block can shift or tilt. Control points with known easting, northing and RL tie the model to the site datum and allow its accuracy to be proved on independent checkpoints.

beyond: Not for the exam. Continuously operating reference stations now broadcast corrections so that a single GNSS receiver fixes control to a centimetre in minutes, and national networks publish coordinates on a modern reference frame that moves with the tectonic plate. Traverses and levelling are still used where the sky is blocked and for the tightest height work. Search for CORS network, real-time kinematic positioning and ground control point accuracy.
